#6748. Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3837 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3837 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.
  • Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing.
  • Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.

Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.

Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

According to recent reports, our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) indicated that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.

We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:.

Sources indicate that most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.

In a recent development, for this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.

RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.

In a recent development, this section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.

Each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:.

Recent findings suggest that we used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.

Sources indicate that A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:.

Sources indicate that each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:.

Industry observers note that 858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.

A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.

Of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below highlights how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.

Qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.

This example highlights how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.

Industry observers note that the pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

Each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:.

The figure below shows how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.

harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below demonstrates what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.

We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.

For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.

To obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.

The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which demonstrated that 0.1 worked best).

We performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then revealed signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.

In a recent development, each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below indicates the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).

As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.

According to recent reports, the final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:.

Sources indicate that before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.

Industry observers note that we also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.

The number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.

Industry observers note that merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?

Recent findings suggest that we started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.

We concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each upgrade below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:.

Industry observers note that the plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own update. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.

Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):.

"Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.

With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).

Despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.

Use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.

Recent findings suggest that the super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.

According to recent reports, the ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.

This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.

Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.

Recent findings suggest that during training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets fresh tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.

Industry observers note that on the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.

This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.

We evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi automatically applies context compaction, while OpenCode and Hermes don't, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.

Industry observers note that every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.

For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.

For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.

All three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).

Industry observers note that the adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.

To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.

Industry observers note that under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.

What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?

Recent findings suggest that we ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?

According to recent reports, results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.

We appreciate the feedback from the people and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.

Recent findings suggest that this question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.

In a recent development, this phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.

In a recent development, does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.

However this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.

Industry observers note that throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.

In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.

Sources indicate that we also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

View CSAF Summary Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to retrieve sensitive system information, access application data without authorization, recover stored credentials, or intercept and manipulate network communications. The following versions of Dorsett Controls InfoScan are affected: InfoScan <=1.45.0 (CVE-2026-117659, CVE-2026-120157, CVE-2026-120255, CVE-2026-120260, CVE-2026-120271, CVE-2026-120298) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 8.1 Dorsett Controls InfoScan 5 Vulnerabilities Improper Certificate Validation, Exposure of Sensitive System Information to an Unauthorized Control Sphere, Use of Hard-coded Cryptographic Key, Missing Authentication for Critical Function, Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Water and Wastewater Systems Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: United States Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-117659 The InfoScan Electron desktop client improperly handles TLS certificate errors by accepting certificates without validating their trustworthiness. The client also configures Electron with nodeIntegration enabled, contextIsolation disabled, and webSecurity disabled. These settings weaken the client’s security boundaries. An attacker who is able to intercept or manipulate network communications may be able to present an untrusted certificate without the application rejecting the connection. Read More 1 Affected Product Dorsett Controls InfoScan <=1.45.0 Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fixDorsett Controls recommends updating affected versions of InfoScan to v1.46 or higher. To install the security patch, user administrators will need to log in to InfoScan and select System Maintenance from the menu. Once the System Maintenance application is open, select Check for Updates, and click the Install Now button in the Ready To Install section. If you are an offline customer (InfoScan has no internet access), you will need to download the enhancement from the Dorsett Controls Customer Portal by selecting the InfoScan Update tile, downloading the update, and following the instructions listed on the portal. Recommended Practices CISA recommends consumers take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams. Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks. No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time. Upcoming in AWS Quick: More capable flows, an updated web experience, and agents that work together

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Turn one person’s process into your team’s process, get more done in the Quick web app, and get more complete answers from agents working together.
  • AWS Quick is the AI workspace built only for work.
  • Industry observers note that AI assistants make individuals faster, but the gains often stay with one person.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turn one person’s process into your team’s process, get more done in the Quick web app, and get more complete answers from agents working together.

AWS Quick is the AI workspace built only for work. Today, we are releasing updates that help your team get more of its everyday work done:.

Industry observers note that AI assistants make individuals faster, but the gains often stay with one person. The way one analyst builds the monthly report rarely becomes the way the team builds it, and work waits until someone is back at their desk. This release helps your team turn what one person knows into a process everyone can rely on, and keeps work moving when you step away.

Industry observers note that AWS Quick Flows already helps teams automate and standardize business processes so people can focus on their most important work. Now you can build, run, and refine flows entirely in chat. And your flows can take on more of your tough work, whether you start it from the web, desktop, or mobile app.

Recent findings suggest that for example, here is how flows could support a finance team. Maya is a financial planning and analysis manager at a retailer. Each month, she prepares a report for her VP of Finance that explains changes to costs and margins. For each region, she pulls last month’s results, compares them to the plan in a spreadsheet, writes commentary on the biggest changes, and sends the report. The process lives in her memory and a personal checklist. When she is out, a teammate has to rebuild the report from scratch, and it looks different every time.

With Quick, Maya can standardize the process, automate it, and make it available to her team. She describes her process in chat, the way she would explain it to a new employee. Quick builds the flow from her description and she tests and refines it in the same conversation. A diagram beside the chat demonstrates each step, so she can confirm it matches how she works.

It has been revealed that figure 1: Maya describes her monthly report in chat, and Quick builds the flow with a diagram beside it. Both views, enlarged here for visibility, appear side by side in the same Quick window.

Industry observers note that A flow can now bring together agents, skills, tools, and data, and handle longer processes with more data. Fixed calculations and checks keep the results consistent, agents draft and analyze, and Maya decides what goes in the final report. On each run, her flow:.

It has been revealed that maya publishes the flow for her team. At the next month-end, she is at a planning meeting, so Jordan, an analyst on her team, runs it from chat in the Quick desktop app. There, the flow can use a spreadsheet of regional adjustments saved on his computer. Before the report goes out, Jordan reviews the draft, including why each region was flagged, asks for a few changes in chat, and approves it for the VP of Finance. When Priya joins the team, she runs the same flow at her first month-end, and the report is built the same way.

While this is a fictional example, real customers tell us they’re automating complex business processes to make them more consistent and repeatable. This gives their people back valuable time to focus on more strategic work. Take Pomelo, a Latin American fintech provider powering card issuance, processing, and payment operations for customers:.

It has been revealed that “At Pomelo, AWS Quick changed who gets to build solutions. Before, every analysis or automation depended on the data team. Today, people across every area explore information, make decisions, and build their own agents and flows within a unified, governed environment. Without growing our team, nearly four times as many people now work with data each month, so our data team can focus on its most complex, high-impact work. A single use case already saves us 80 hours of work per month. But the real transformation isn’t the hours we save. Quick is transforming our data and innovation culture: we’ve gone from a few people building solutions for many to an organization where everyone can create, experiment, and change the way they work. And we’re just getting started.”.

— Rodrigo Marini, Head of Data, Pomelo Fintech Services S.A.S.

Sources indicate that if you already use Quick in your browser, the updated web app puts the items that need your attention on the home screen as soon as you sign in. A reorganized left navigation brings agents, flows, skills, knowledge, and connectors together under Customize. It includes the agents and skills you built on desktop and ones others have shared with you. Your existing dashboards, topics, and spaces work as before, and you do not need to turn anything on.

Figure 2: The feed brings the morning’s email and messages that need a reply into one view.

In a recent development, some requests need the knowledge of more than one specialized agent. With multi-agent orchestration, the agent you ask can bring in several specialized agents at once, each working on the part it knows best. The agent then combines their work into one response. Each agent keeps its own instructions, knowledge, and context, so the people who know that work best can build and maintain it.

In a recent development, for example, you might ask why shipping costs rose in one region. Your agent can bring in a forecasting agent built on your team’s planning data and a procurement agent built on the procurement team’s vendor contracts. You get one response that demonstrates what each agent contributed, and you decide what to do with it.

Work lives in many systems. This release adds new connectors so Quick can pull from the analytics and tools your team uses every day. Connect once, then ask in natural language.

Sources indicate that meta ads. Create, manage, and analyze Meta ad campaigns in natural language through a connector to Meta’s ads Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. Quick combines Meta ad data with your first-party and third-party sources, and asks for your permission before it creates a campaign, changes a budget, or takes any other write action in an ad account. Try Quick free for 3 months and invite up to 10 teammates at no cost.

Industry observers note that amplitude. Ask about product usage, customer behavior, and conversion in natural language. Quick connects to Amplitude through its MCP server, so product and marketing teams can pull behavioral insights into the dashboards, documents, and workflows they build in Quick.

Connectors respect your existing permissions. Quick only demonstrates each person what they already have access to. Quick asks before it takes any write action. Administrators choose which connectors teams can add.

It has been revealed that whether you build a monthly report, run one your manager built, or set up Quick for your organization, Quick works the way you do. Your data stays in your environment and does not train anyone else’s models. You bring the judgment, and Quick gives your team the capacity to match its goals.

These features are available today in all Regions where AWS Quick is available.

It has been revealed that to try what’s latest, sign in to Quick or download Quick and get started in minutes. To learn about enterprise pricing intends, talk to your AWS account team.

Industry observers note that view CSAF Summary Simcenter Femap is affected by an out of bounds read vulnerability that could be triggered when the application reads files in X_T format. This could allow an attacker to crash the application or execute arbitrary code. Siemens has released a new version for Simcenter Femap and recommends to revision to the latest version. The following versions of Siemens Simcenter Femap are affected: Simcenter Femap vers:intdot/<2606.0002 (CVE-2026-64629) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 7.8 Siemens Simcenter Femap 1 Vulnerability Out-of-bounds Read Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-64629 The affected applications contains an out of bounds read vulnerability while parsing specially crafted X_T files. This could allow an attacker to execute code in the context of the current process. Read More 1 Affected Product Simcenter Femap < V2606.0002 Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fixUpdate to V2606.0002 or later version Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-125 Out-of-bounds Read CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 7.8 HIGH CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H View CVE Details Acknowledgments Siemens ProductCERT reported this vulnerability to CISA. General Recommendations As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Recommended Practices CISA recommends consumers take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. Susana Barraza is the NICE Program Manager at NIST. She previously served as the Student Personnel Assistant for the HSI STEM Equity and Success Initiative (SESI) Project at Sacramento City College. She has also participated in a Political Management Seminar at The George Washington University as a component of a fellowship with the Congressional Hispanic Leadership Institute in Washington, DC. Additionally, Susana served as an intern for Ford Motor Company, the House of Representatives, and for the California State Assembly.

Susana earned an Associates of Science in Business Administration and an Associates of Arts in Interdisciplinary Studies- Social and Behavioral Sciences. Then Susana transferred to California State University, Sacramento (CSUS) where she received a Bachelor’s in Economics with a minor in Business Administration. She is a 2020 Pathway Fellow Recipient with the College of Education at CSUS; a program (1 out of 6 nationwide) that prepares highly qualified diverse participants for doctorates and careers in rigorous educational research. In 2026, Susana completed a Master's in education, with a focus on organizational leadership and learning at The George Washington University.

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.
  • CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.
  • These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2024-10441 Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM) Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output Vulnerability CVE-2026-40217 BerriAI LiteLLM Unprotected Alternate Channel Vulnerability CVE-2026-90436 Apache Axis Unsafe Reflection Vulnerability CVE-2026-90817 Vanderbilt University Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) Code Injection Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

#6683. Latest Update: Fine-tuning LLMs to 1.58bit: extreme quantization made easy

📅 18 Sep 2024 • ⏱️ 21m • 📚 Deep Dive (4118 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Fine-tuning LLMs to 1.58bit: extreme quantization made easy

📅 18 Sep 2024 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4118 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As Large Language Models (LLMs) grow in size and complexity, finding ways to reduce their computational and energy costs has become a critical challenge.
  • BitNet is a special transformers architecture that represents each parameter with only three values: (-1, 0, 1), offering a extreme quantization of just 1.58 ( log2(3) log_2(3) log2​(3) ) bits per parameter.
  • In a recent development, bitNet is an architecture introduced by Microsoft Research that uses extreme quantization, representing each parameter with only three values: -1, 0, and 1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As Large Language Models (LLMs) grow in size and complexity, finding ways to reduce their computational and energy costs has become a critical challenge. One popular solution is quantization, where the precision of parameters is reduced from the standard 16-bit floating-point (FP16) or 32-bit floating-point (FP32) to lower-bit formats like 8-bit or 4-bit. While this approach significantly cuts down on memory usage and speeds up computation, it often comes at the expense of accuracy. Reducing the precision too much can cause models to lose crucial information, resulting in degraded performance.

BitNet is a special transformers architecture that represents each parameter with only three values: (-1, 0, 1), offering a extreme quantization of just 1.58 ( log2(3) log_2(3) log2​(3) ) bits per parameter. However, it requires to train a model from scratch. While the results are impressive, not everybody has the budget to pre-train an LLM. To overcome this limitation, we explored a few tricks that allow fine-tuning an existing model to 1.58 bits! Keep reading to find out how !

In a recent development, bitNet is an architecture introduced by Microsoft Research that uses extreme quantization, representing each parameter with only three values: -1, 0, and 1. This results in a model that uses just 1.58 bits per parameter, significantly reducing computational and memory requirements.

This architecture uses INT8 addition calculations when performing matrix multiplication, in contrast to LLaMA LLM's FP16 addition and multiplication operations.

This results in a theoretically reduced energy consumption, with BitNet b1.58 saving 71.4 times the arithmetic operations energy for matrix multiplication compared to the Llama baseline.

According to recent reports, we have successfully fine-tuned a Llama3 8B model using the BitNet architecture, achieving strong performance on downstream tasks. The 8B models we developed are released under the HF1BitLLM organization. Two of these models were fine-tuned on 10B tokens with different training setup, while the third was fine-tuned on 100B tokens. Notably, our models surpass the Llama 1 7B model in MMLU benchmarks.

Recent findings suggest that to integrate the BitNet architecture into Transformers, we introduced a new quantization method called "bitnet" (PR). This method involves replacing the standard Linear layers with specialized BitLinear layers that are compatible with the BitNet architecture, with appropriate dynamic quantization of activations, weight unpacking, and matrix multiplication.

Loading and testing the model in Transformers is incredibly straightforward, there are zero changes to the API:.

With this code, everything is managed seamlessly behind the scenes, so there's no need to worry about additional complexities, you just need to install the latest version of transformers.

For a quick test of the model, check out this notebook.

BitNet replaces traditional Linear layers in Multi-Head Attention and Feed-Forward Networks with specialized layers called BitLinear that use ternary precision (or even binary, in the initial version). The BitLinear layers we use in this project quantize the weights using ternary precision (with values of -1, 0, and 1), and we quantize the activations to 8-bit precision. We use a different implementation of BitLinear for training than we do for inference, as we'll see in the next section.

The main obstacle to training in ternary precision is that the weight values are discretized (via the round() function) and thus non-differentiable. BitLinear solves this with a nice trick: STE (Straight Through Estimator). The STE allows gradients to flow through the non-differentiable rounding operation by approximating its gradient as 1 (treating round() as equivalent to the identity function). Another way to view it is that, instead of stopping the gradient at the rounding step, the STE lets the gradient pass through as if the rounding never occurred, enabling weight updates using standard gradient-based optimization techniques.

We train in full precision, but quantize the weights into ternary values as we go, using symmetric per tensor quantization. First, we compute the average of the absolute values of the weight matrix and use this as a scale. We then divide the weights by the scale, round the values, constrain them between -1 and 1, and finally rescale them to continue in full precision.

scalew=11nm∑ij∣Wij∣ scale_w = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{nm} \sum_{ij} |W_{ij}|} scalew​=nm1​∑ij​∣Wij​∣1​.

Wq=clamp[−1,1](round(W∗scale)) W_q = \text{clamp}_{[-1,1]}(\text{round}(W*scale)) Wq​=clamp[−1,1]​(round(W∗scale)).

Wdequantized=Wq∗scalew W_{dequantized} = W_q*scale_w Wdequantized​=Wq​∗scalew​.

It has been revealed that activations are then quantized to a specified bit-width (8-bit, in our case) using absmax per token quantization (for a comprehensive introduction to quantization methods check out this post). This involves scaling the activations into the range [−128, 127] for an 8-bit bit-width. The quantization formula is:.

scalex=127∣X∣max, dim=−1 scale_x = \frac{127}{|X|_{\text{max}, \, \text{dim}=-1}} scalex​=∣X∣max,dim=−1​127​.

Xq=clamp[−128,127](round(X∗scale)) X_q = \text{clamp}_{[-128,127]}(\text{round}(X*scale)) Xq​=clamp[−128,127]​(round(X∗scale)).

Xdequantized=Xq∗scalex X_{dequantized} = X_q * scale_x Xdequantized​=Xq​∗scalex​.

We apply Layer Normalization (LN) before quantizing the activations to maintain the variance of the output:.

LN(x)=x−E(x)Var(x)+ϵ \text{LN}(x) = \frac{x - E(x)}{\sqrt{\text{Var}(x) + \epsilon}} LN(x)=Var(x)+ϵ​x−E(x)​.

where ϵ is a small number to prevent overflow.

The round() function is not differentiable, as mentioned before. We use detach() as a trick to implement a differentiable straight-through estimator in the backward pass:.

During inference, we simply quantize the weights to ternary values without rescaling. We apply the same approach to activations using 8-bit precision, then perform a matrix multiplication with an efficient kernel, followed by dividing by both the weight and activation scales. This should significantly improve inference speed, particularly with optimized hardware. You can see that the rescaling process differs during training, as matrix multiplications are kept in fp16/bf16/fp32 for proper training.

According to recent reports, before attempting fine-tuning, we first tried to reproduce the results of the BitNet paper with pre-training. We started with a small dataset, tinystories, and a Llama3 8B model. We confirmed that adding a normalization function, like the paper does, improves performance. For example, after 2000 steps of training, we had a perplexity on the validation set equal to 6.3 without normalization, and 5.9 with normalization. Training was stable in both cases.

While this approach looks very interesting for pre-training, only a few institutions can afford doing it at the necessary scale. However, there is already a wide range of strong pretrained models, and it would be extremely useful if they could be converted to 1.58bit after pre-training. Other groups had reported that fine-tuning results were not as strong as those achieved with pre-training, so we set out on an investigation to see if we could make 1.58 fine-tuning work.

When we began fine-tuning from the pre-trained Llama3 8B weights, the model performed slightly better but not as well as we expected.

It has been revealed that note: All our experiments were conducted using Nanotron. If you're interested in trying 1.58bit pre-training or fine-tuning, you can check out this PR.

To understand why, we tried to inspect both the weight distributions of the randomly initialized model and the pre-trained model to identify potential problems.

And the scale values for the two distributions are, respectively :.

The initial random weight distribution is a mix of two normal distributions:.

Industry observers note that this results from using different stds for column linear and row linear weights in nanotron. In the quantized version, all matrices have only 2 weight scales (50.25 and 402), which are the inverse of the mean absolute value of the weights for each matrix: scale = 1.0 / w.abs().mean().clamp_(min=1e-5).

On the other hand, the pretrained weight's distribution looks like a normal distribution with an std=0.013 \text{std} = 0.013 std=0.013.

According to recent reports, clearly, the pretrained model starts with more information (scales), while the randomly initialized model starts with practically no information and adds to it over time. Our conclusion was that starting with random weights gives the model minimal initial information, enabling a gradual learning process, while during fine-tuning, the introduction of BitLinear layers overwhelms the model into losing all its prior information.

Recent findings suggest that to improve the fine-tuning results, we tried different techniques. For example, instead of using per-tensor quantization, we tried per-row and per-column quantization to keep more information from the Llama 3 weights. We also tried to change the way the scale is computed: instead of just taking the mean absolute value of the weights as a scale, we take the mean absolute value of the outliers as a scale (an outlier value is a value that exceeds k*mean_absolute_value, where k is a constant we tried to vary in our experiments), but we didn’t notice significant improvements.

In a recent development, we observed that both the random weights and the Llama 3 weights resulted in losses starting at approximately the same value of 13. This suggests that the Llama 3 model loses all of its prior information when quantization is introduced. To further investigate how much information the model loses during this process, we experimented with per-group quantization.

Sources indicate that as a sanity check, we first set the group size to 1, which essentially means no quantization. In this scenario, the loss started at 1.45, same as we see during normal fine-tuning. However, when we increased the group size to 2, the loss jumped to around 11. This indicates that even with a minimal group size of 2, the model still loses nearly all of its information.

Recent findings suggest that to address this issue, we considered the possibility of introducing quantization gradually rather than applying it abruptly to the weights and activations for each tensor. To achieve this, we implemented a lambda value to control the process :.

When lambda is set to 0, there is essentially no quantization occurring, while at lambda=1, full quantization is applied.

We initially tested some discrete lambda values, such as 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, and 1. However, this approach did not lead to any significant improvement in results, mainly because lambda=0.25 is already high enough for the loss to start very high.

As a result, we decided to experiment with a lambda value that adjusts dynamically based on the training step.

According to recent reports, using this dynamic lambda value led to better loss convergence, but the perplexity (ppl) results during inference, when lambda was set to 1, were still far from satisfactory. We realized this was likely because the model hadn't been trained long enough with lambda=1. To address this, we adjusted our lambda value to improve the training process.

With this configuration, after 2000 steps we have :.

Our fine-tuning method indicates better convergence overall. You can observe a slight increase in the loss curve around 1,000 steps, which corresponds to when we begin approaching lambda=1, or full quantization. However, immediately after this point, the loss starts to converge again, leading to an improved perplexity of approximately 4.

According to recent reports, despite this progress, when we tested the quantized model on the WikiText dataset (instead of the tinystories one we used for fine-tuning), it showed a very high perplexity. This suggests that fine-tuning the model in low-bit mode on a specific dataset causes it to lose much of its general knowledge. This matter might arise because the minimal representations we aim for with ternary weights can vary significantly from one dataset to another. To address this problem, we scaled our training process to include the larger FineWeb-edu dataset. We maintained a lambda value of:.

We chose this lambda value because it seemed to be a good starting point for warming up the model. We then trained the model using a learning rate of 1e-4 for 5,000 steps on the FineWeb-edu dataset. The training involved a batch size (BS) of 2 million, totaling 10 billion tokens.

Finding the right learning rate and the right decay was challenging; it seems to be a crucial factor in the model's performance.

After the fine-tuning process on Fineweb-Edu, the perplexity on the WikiText dataset reached 12.2, which is quite impressive given that we only used 10 billion tokens. The other evaluation metrics also show strong performance considering the limited amount of data (see results).

We also tried to smooth out the sharp increase when lambda approaches 1. To do this, we considered using lambda schedulers that grow exponentially at first, then level off as they get closer to 1.

for different k values, with a number of total warmup steps of 1, we have plots like the following :.

We ran 4 experiments using the best-performing learning rate of 1e-4, testing values of k in [4, 6, 8, 10].

In a recent development, the smoothing worked well, as there's no spike like with the linear scheduler. However, the perplexity isn't great, staying around ~15, and the performance on downstream tasks is not better.

We also noticed the spike at the beginning, which the model struggled to recover from. With lambda = 0, there's essentially no quantization, so the loss starts low, around ~2. But right after the first step, there's a spike, similar to what happened with the linear scheduler (as seen in the blue plot above). So, we tried a different scheduler—a sigmoid one—that starts slowly, rises sharply to 1, and then levels off as it approaches 1.

For different k values we have the following curves :.

We ran 5 experiments this time with k in [15, 20, 25, 40, 100] :.

Sources indicate that the sharp increase in lambda caused instability around the 500th step and didn’t fix the first divergence issue. However, for k=100 k = 100 k=100, we observed some improvement in downstream tasks (see the results table), although perplexity remained around ~13.5. Despite this, it didn’t show a clear performance boost over a linear scheduler.

In a recent development, additionally, we experimented with training models from scratch using random weights and various learning rates. This allowed us to compare the effectiveness of our fine-tuning approach against traditional pre-training methods.

It has been revealed that none of the models trained from random weights performed better than our fine-tuned model. The best perplexity we achieved with those models was 26, which falls short compared to the results from our fine-tuning approach.

We scaled our experiments to 100 billion tokens to see if we could match the performance of Llama 3 8B. We conducted longer training runs, starting from our best-performing checkpoint from the shorter runs with the linear scheduler, and continued fine-tuning for 45,000 steps. We experimented with different learning rates, and while the model performed closely to the Llama 3 model in some metrics, on average, it still lagged behind.

Here are some examples of the metrics we evaluated at various checkpoints during the training :.

and the average score looks like :.

Industry observers note that in our initial experiments with smaller models like SmolLM, we observed that the warmup quantization technique didn’t yield as much improvement as it did with larger models. This suggests that the effectiveness of warmup quantization could be more closely related to model size and complexity.

Industry observers note that for example, here are the loss curves for the SmolLM 135M model, comparing warmup quantization with full quantization from the start. Interestingly, the curves closely align, and the resulting perplexities aren't significantly different.

BitNet is effective in delivering strong performance compared to baseline methods, especially at lower bit levels. According to the paper, BitNet achieves scores that are on par with 8-bit models but with significantly lower inference costs. In the case of 4-bit models, methods that only quantize weights outperform those that quantize both weights and activations, as activations are harder to quantify. However, BitNet, which uses 1.58-bit weights, surpasses both weight-only and weight-and-activation quantization methods.

The table below presents the results for various metrics after the 10B fine-tuning process of Llama3 8B. These results are compared against those from other model architectures to provide a comprehensive overview of performance (All evaluations were conducted using Lighteval on the Nanotron format model).

In a recent development, after fine-tuning on just 10 billion tokens using ternary weights, the model demonstrates impressive performance, especially when compared to other models that underwent much more extensive training. For instance, it outperforms the Bitnet 7B model, which was trained on a significantly larger dataset of 100 billion tokens. Additionally, it performs better than the FBI LLM (Fully Binarized LLM), a model that was distilled on an even more massive 1.26 trillion tokens. This highlights the model's efficiency and effectiveness despite the relatively smaller scale of its fine-tuning process.

For the 100B tokens experiments, the best performing checkpoint we had is the following :.

To replicate these results, you can check out this PR to convert models to nanotron format, unpack the weights (check the function unpack_weights), and use lighteval.

Note that even though the models are fine-tuned from an Instruct-tuned model, they still need to be fine-tuned using an Instruct dataset as well. These can be considered base models.

Recent findings suggest that to benefit from the BitNet low-precision weights, we pack them into an int8 tensor (this makes the number of parameters go from 8B to 2.8B!). During inference, these weights must be unpacked before performing matrix multiplication. We implemented custom kernels in Cuda and Triton to handle the on-the-fly unpacking during the matrix multiplication process. For the matrix multiplication itself, we employed the cached tiled matrix multiplication technique. To fully grasp this approach, let's first review some Cuda programming fundamentals.

Before diving into cached tiled matrix multiplication, it's important to understand some basic GPU concepts:.

A simple implementation of matrix multiplication on a GPU might involve each thread computing a single element of the result matrix by directly reading the necessary elements from global memory. However, this approach can be inefficient for the following reasons:.

Tiling is a technique used to address these challenges, and it was mainly used in FlashAttention to improve the kernel's efficiency. The basic idea is to divide the matrices into smaller sub-matrices, called tiles, which can fit into the shared memory of the GPU. Instead of computing the entire output matrix in one go, the computation is broken down into smaller pieces that are processed tile by tile.

It has been revealed that in the context of matrix multiplication, this means dividing matrices A and B into blocks (tiles), loading these tiles into shared memory, and then performing the multiplication on these smaller blocks. This approach allows the threads to reuse data stored in the fast shared memory, reducing the need to access global memory repeatedly.

When implementing cached tiled matrix multiplication, several factors are considered:.

Here is the kernel in triton we benchmarked :.

The kernel first determines which tile (block) of the output matrix each thread block is responsible for:.

The kernel uses a loop to iterate over the K dimension in chunks of BLOCK_SIZE_K. For each chunk:.

After all tiles along the K dimension have been processed, the final results stored in the accumulator are converted to float16 and written back to the corresponding tile of matrix C in global memory. The writing process respects memory boundaries using a mask to ensure that only valid elements are written.

For a more detailed explanation of the code, checkout this PR.

Recent findings suggest that we benchmarked our kernel against the method of unpacking the weights using @torch.compile followed by performing the matmul in BF16 precision, and found that both approaches achieved approximately the same performance. To ensure accurate benchmarking, we performed the matmul operation over 2000 iterations and averaged the time taken during the last 1000 iterations, to eliminate any inefficiencies related to initial loading or compilation. Below is a graph showing the benchmark results. We also tested various matrix sizes, with the x-axis representing the number of multiplications on a log scale, and the y-axis showing the average time in ms.

Industry observers note that we also tried using BitBlas, which is a software library designed to perform matrix operations with mixed precision. It helps optimize these operations by allowing calculations to be done in lower precision formats like INT8, INT4, or even INT2, instead of the traditional FP32 or FP16 formats.

The benchmark results are promising, as BitBlas outperforms both our custom kernel and Torch's matmul function in low precision, as shown in the graph.

However, during model loading, BitBlas needs to compile kernels tailored to the shape of the weight matrix and store them in a local database, which can increase the initial loading time.

Recent findings suggest that in conclusion, as LLMs continue to expand, reducing their computational demands through quantization is essential. This blog has explored the approach of 1.58-bit quantization, which uses ternary weights. While pre-training models in 1.58 bits is resource-intensive, we’ve demonstrated that, with some tricks, it’s possible to fine-tune existing models to this precision level, achieving efficient performance without sacrificing accuracy. By optimizing inference speed through specialized kernels, BitNet opens fresh possibilities for making LLMs more practical and scalable.

We would like to express our sincere gratitude to Leandro von Werra, Thomas Wolf, and Marc Sun for their invaluable assistance and insights throughout this project. We also extend our thanks to Omar Sanseviero and Pedro Cuenca for their contributions in refining this blog post, helping to communicate our findings clearly and effectively to the AI community. Furthermore, we want to acknowledge the GeneralAI team for their pioneering work on the BitNet project. Their research has been foundational to our efforts, and we are particularly grateful for the clear and precise figures provided in their paper.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, deploying Transformers models at the edge or client-side requires careful consideration of performance and compatibility. Python, though powerful, is not always ideal for such deployments, especially in environments dominated by C++. This blog will guide you through optimizing and deploying Hugging Face Transformers models using Optimum-Intel and OpenVINO™ GenAI, ensuring efficient AI inference with minimal dependencies.

Industry observers note that openVINO™ was originally developed as a C++ AI inference solution, making it ideal for edge and client deployment where minimizing dependencies is crucial. With the introduction of the GenAI API, integrating large language models (LLMs) into C++ or Python applications has become even more straightforward, with features designed to simplify deployment and enhance performance.

In a recent development, to start, ensure your environment is properly configured with both Python and C++. Install the necessary Python packages:.

Here are the specific packages used in this blog post:.

For GenAI C++ libraries installation follow the instruction here.

Industry observers note that hugging Face and Intel's collaboration has led to the Optimum-Intel project. It is designed to optimize Transformers models for inference on Intel HW. Optimum-Intel supports OpenVINO as an inference backend and its API has wrappers for various model architectures built on top of OpenVINO inference API. All of these wrappers start from OV prefix, for example, OVModelForCausalLM. Otherwise, it is similar to the API of 🤗 Transformers library.

In a recent development, to export Transformers models to OpenVINO Intermediate Representation (IR) one can use two options: This can be done using Python’s .from_pretrained() method or the Optimum command-line interface (CLI). Below are examples using both methods:.

In a recent development, the ./llama-3.1-8b-ov folder will contain .xml and bin IR model files and required configuration files that come from the source model. 🤗 tokenizer will be also converted to the format of openvino-tokenizers library and corresponding configuration files will be created in the same folder.

When running LLMs on the resource constrained edge and client devices, model optimization is highly recommended step. Weight-only quantization is a mainstream approach that significantly reduces latency and model footprint. Optimum-Intel offers weight-only quantization through the Neural Network Compression Framework (NNCF), which has a variety of optimization techniques designed specifically for LLMs: from data-free INT8 and INT4 weight quantization to data-aware methods such as AWQ, GPTQ, quantization scale estimation, mixed-precision quantization. By default, weights of the models that are larger than one billion parameters are quantized to INT8 precision which is safe in terms of accuracy. It means that the export steps described above lead to the model with 8-bit weights. However, 4-bit integer weight-only quantization allows achieving a better accuracy-performance trade-off.

It has been revealed that for meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B model we recommend stacking AWQ, quantization scale estimation along with mixed-precision INT4/INT8 quantization of weights using a calibration dataset that reflects a deployment use case. As in the case of export, there are two options on how to apply 4-bit weight-only quantization to LLM model:.

Note: The model optimization process can take time as it and applies several methods subsequently and uses model inference over the specified dataset.

Model optimization with API is more flexible as it allows using custom datasets that can be passed as an iterable object, for example, and instance of Dataset object of 🤗 library or just a list of strings.

Weight quantization usually introduces some degradation of the accuracy metric. To compare optimized and source models we report Word Perplexity metric measured on the Wikitext dataset with lm-evaluation-harness project which support both 🤗 Transformers and Optimum-Intel models out-of-the-box.

After conversion and optimization, deploying the model using OpenVINO GenAI is straightforward. The LLMPipeline class in OpenVINO GenAI provides both Python and C++ APIs, supporting various text generation methods with minimal dependencies.

To run this example you need minimum dependencies to be installed into the Python environment as OpenVINO GenAI is designed to provide a lightweight deployment. You can install OpenVINO GenAI package to the same Python environment or create a separate one to compare the application footprint:.

Let's see how to run the same pipeline with OpenVINO GenAI C++ API. The GenAI API is designed to be intuitive and provides a seamless migration from 🤗 Transformers API.

Note: In the below example, any other available device in your environment can be specified for "device" variable. For example, if you are using an Intel CPU with integrated graphics, "GPU" is a good option to try with. To check the available devices, you can use ov::Core::get_available_devices method (refer to query-device-properties).

LLMPipeline also allows specifying custom generation options by means of ov::genai::GenerationConfig:.

With the LLMPipieline, owners can not only effortlessly leverage various decoding algorithms such as Beam Search but also construct an interactive chat scenario with a Streamer as in the below example. Moreover, one can take advantage of enhanced internal optimizations with LLMPipeline, such as reduced prompt processing time with utilization of KV cache of previous chat history with the chat methods : start_chat() and finish_chat() (refer to using-genai-in-chat-scenario).

And finally let's see how to use LLMPipeline in the chat scenario:.

The combination of Optimum-Intel and OpenVINO™ GenAI offers a powerful, flexible solution for deploying Hugging Face models at the edge. By following these steps, you can achieve optimized, high-performance AI inference in environments where Python may not be ideal, ensuring your applications run smoothly across Intel hardware.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that however, many people may not have fully explored all of the features Daily Papers offers.
  • On the Daily Papers page, you’ll notice author names listed under the title of each paper.
  • This feature makes it easy for the community to connect with you and your work, creating more opportunities for collaboration and interaction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that however, many people may not have fully explored all of the features Daily Papers offers. This article will guide you through some hidden functionalities to help you make the most of this platform.

On the Daily Papers page, you’ll notice author names listed under the title of each paper. If you're one of the authors and have a Hugging Face account, you can claim your paper with a single click! After claiming, the paper will be automatically linked to your account, adding visibility to your research and helping build your personal brand in the community.

This feature makes it easy for the community to connect with you and your work, creating more opportunities for collaboration and interaction.

It has been revealed that the paper submission feature is open to all users who’ve claimed a paper. Users don’t have to limit submissions to their own work, they can also share interesting research papers that would benefit the community.

This allows Hugging Face Papers to maintain an up-to-date and ever-expanding collection of research in the AI field, curated by the community!

Recent findings suggest that under each paper, there is a discussion section where people can leave comments and engage in direct conversations with the authors. Tagging the authors (@username) can lead to real-time feedback, questions or discussion of the research.

In a recent development, this feature fosters interaction, bringing together researchers from the whole community. Everyone, from beginners to experts, can contribute their ideas, making the global AI community even more connected and inclusive.

Whether to ask clarification questions or share constructive feedback, it opens the door to meaningful dialogue and can even spark new ideas or collaborations.

On each paper’s page, you’ll find related resources, such as models, datasets, demos and other useful collections, all linked on the right side.

Recent findings suggest that authors can easily associate their models or datasets with their paper by simply adding the paper's arXiv URL to the README.md file of their resources. This feature allows authors to highlight their work and helps users access everything they need in one convenient place.

In a recent development, you can support the paper by clicking the upvote button in the top-right corner. This allows the community to recommend the paper and support the author's work. The upvote feature highlights influential and innovative research, helping more people discover and focus on excellent papers.

For authors, each upvote acts as a recognition of their efforts and can be a source of motivation to continue producing high-quality research.

If you type @librarian-bot in the comment section, the system will automatically suggest related papers. This feature is great for those looking to dive deeper into a topic or explore similar ideas. It’s like having a personal AI-powered research assistant!

At Hugging Face, we value diversity, and that extends to language as well. On the Daily Papers page, consumers can leave comments in any language, and our built-in translation feature will ensure everyone can understand and contribute.

Whether you’re providing feedback, discussing a question, or exchanging ideas, this feature helps break down language barriers, making global collaboration even easier.

This feature makes it easy to browse the latest titles at a glance and jump into any research that catches your eye.

In a recent development, there’s also some cool integration between Paper Pages and arXiv. For example, you can easily check if a paper on arXiv has already been featured on Hugging Face's Daily Papers page. If you spot the familiar emoji 🤗 on the page, you can click it to jump straight to the paper page on Daily Papers and explore all the features mentioned above.

To use the arXiv to HF Paper Pages feature, you'll need to install an extention, which you can find here: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/arxiv-to-hf/icfbnjkijgggnhmlikeppnoehoalpcpp.

Sources indicate that on arXiv, you can also check if a paper has a demo hosted on Hugging Face Spaces. If the author has added a link, you can click it to jump directly to the Space and try out the demo yourself!

In a recent development, we hope this guide helps you make the most of Daily Papers on Hugging Face. By utilizing all these features, you can stay up-to-date with the latest research, engage with authors, and contribute to the growing AI community. Whether you're a researcher, developer or curious beginner, Daily Papers is here to help you connect with the top AI research!
